answer: STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, real pain point with first-hand validation: 212-person survey (78% bills higher than expected, 9% know why) and a genuine split-incentive problem between renters and landlords. (2) Demonstrated traction for a student team: working prototype, 41 pilot apartments, 27 paying users, a paid 12-unit landlord pilot, 400+ waitlist, ~$2,300 revenue. Willingness to pay is partially proven. (3) Measured outcomes: before/after rescans showing ~14% reduction in temperature loss and self-reported 8-12% bill drops; closed-loop verification is a real differentiator versus checklists and thermal cameras. (4) Positive unit economics at kit level: $59 price vs ~$24 COGS (~59% gross margin, improving to ~70% at scale), plus reusable sensors that suit a landlord subscription. (5) Capable, complementary team covering hardware, data/modeling, product design and customer development, with relevant advisors (building energy faculty, veteran property manager). (6) Capital-efficient: only ~$9k spent to reach this stage; sensible use of funds (production run, certification, legal). (7) Multiple potential revenue streams and a plausible data moat over time. WEAKNESSES: (1) Evidence base is thin: 41 users, self-reported bill savings, no control group, one winter, and a 14% reduction at problem points is not the same as whole-unit energy savings; payback and retention are unproven. (2) Market sizing is top-down and generous (12M households x 25% adoption is not a realistic early penetration); hardware is largely one-time purchase with weak repeat demand since the kit is reusable, creating a ceiling on consumer revenue. (3) Landlord side is the weakest link: small landlords are fragmented, hard and costly to reach, and the stated split-incentive problem also means they may not value tenant-paid utility savings; $6/unit/month subscription is unproven (one 12-unit pilot) and may face churn after a seasonal scan. (4) Revenue projections ($85k year one, $420k year two) look aggressive relative to ~$2.3k to date and depend on unproven channels and a utility data pilot; utility sales cycles are long and the data licensing thesis is speculative. (5) Hardware risks: first manufacturing run, certification (FCC/UL) cost and timeline, batch quality, returns, logistics, and the ability to hit $18 COGS at scale; $40k may be tight for 800 kits plus certification, app, legal and marketing. (6) Not yet incorporated, no IP protection described, and defensibility is modest; competitors (smart-home/sensor makers, utility audit programs, cheap thermal cameras, or free utility-provided audits) could replicate with software. (7) Team is all students with limited commercial or hardware-scaling experience, and part-time commitment and post-graduation continuity are unaddressed. (8) Seasonality (winter-only usage) and DIY friction (48-hour sensor placement, renter effort) may limit conversion and repeat engagement. OVERALL: Strong problem fit and unusually good early validation for the stage, but unproven scalability, a tough landlord go-to-market, aggressive projections and hardware execution risk keep this at moderate-to-good seed interest rather than high conviction. Key diligence items: larger controlled pilot, retention and repeat-scan data, landlord CAC and willingness to pay, certified BOM and manufacturing quotes.
